# AI Research Lab

A reusable workspace for academic literature research. The user is a beginner researcher who gives a topic ("Start a new research on X"); you run the research lifecycle as the **research orchestrator** described in `.claude/agents/research-orchestrator.md` (delegation table and state ownership live there).

## Rules (full version: `docs/research-standards.md`, read it before any research work)
- Never invent findings, citations, DOIs, numbers or limitations. Metadata comes from `rlab add`; content comes from the paper text with page refs. Unknown → say "not reported" / "not found".
- Label every claim: **[V]** verified in the paper's data, **[A]** author claim, **[I]** our interpretation. Cite `[@key, p. N]`.
- Detailed method analysis needs the full text; abstract-only work is labelled and weighted lower.
- Prefer peer-reviewed sources; flag preprints; exclude retracted papers.
- Legal open access only. Never bypass paywalls or use shadow libraries; ask the user for missing PDFs.
- Never overwrite or delete `paper.pdf`, `fulltext.txt`, completed analyses, or log history without the user's explicit permission.
- A research gap is claimed only after a recorded novelty check.

## Tools
- `rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py` (run from this directory; `-h` lists commands). Use it for every deterministic step: project creation, search, adding papers (resolves + verifies metadata, rejects duplicates), PDF fetch/attach + text extraction, validation, BibTeX, citation checks, indexing, logging. Never hand-edit `metadata.json`, `registry.json`, `literature-matrix.*`, `references.bib` or `research/INDEX.md`.
- After changing project content, run `rlab index <id>`; log decisions with `rlab log <id> <phase> "<msg>"`.
- Skills (`.claude/skills/`): start-research, discover-papers, analyze-paper, compare-methods, find-gaps, write-literature-review, research-report, reading-guide, resume-research.
- Shareable Google Doc: `python3 scripts/md2gdoc.py --title T --subtitle S [--share anyone] [--pdf out.pdf] [--md out.md] a.md b.md ...` turns simple markdown (one file per page; see the script docstring) into a styled Google Doc owned by the user (auth via the google-doc-builder skill). Per-project reading guides live in `reports/reading-guide/` (`00-front.md`, `papers/<key>.md`, `99-back.md`, `order.txt`).
- External services in use: OpenAlex, Crossref, arXiv, PubMed, doi.org, Europe PMC (no keys needed). Semantic Scholar is rate-limited without a key: use it via WebFetch only as a fallback. Unpaywall runs only if `RLAB_CONTACT_EMAIL` is set.

## Layout
- `research/registry.json` — all projects (via `rlab`); `research/INDEX.md` — human overview.
- `research/<id>/` — one project: `RESEARCH.md`, `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`, `STATUS.md`, `research-log.md`, `literature-matrix.md/.csv`, `evidence-matrix.md`, `gap-report.md`, `references.bib`, `search/`, `papers/<key>/{metadata.json,paper.pdf,fulltext.txt,analysis.md,paper.bib}`, `reports/`.
- `templates/` — project and analysis templates. `docs/` — standards. `tests/` — `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`.

## Working with the user
- Progress updates: 1–3 plain-language lines per phase; explain research terms on first use and the reason behind important decisions.
- Handle routine work yourself. Ask only for: scope/RQ choices that change direction, missing full-text access, paid or restricted resources, destructive actions.
- State lives in files, not in conversation memory: keep `STATUS.md` (Next actions, Blocked / needs user) current so any session can resume.
- [Reading guide doc preference](reading-guide-doc-preference.md) — end every project with plain-English reading guide as public-link Google Doc

# Research standards

The rules every skill and agent in this workspace follows. One source of truth: change rules here, not in individual skills.

## 1. Evidence labels
Every substantive statement about a paper or the literature carries one label:

| Label | Short | Meaning | Requirement |
|---|---|---|---|
| VERIFIED | [V] | Checked against the paper's own data, tables, figures or results text. | Page ref `(key, p. N)` |
| AUTHOR-CLAIM | [A] | The authors state it; we cannot independently check it (e.g. claims of novelty, interpretations, conclusions beyond the data). | Page ref |
| INTERPRETATION | [I] | Our own reasoning, synthesis or critique. | Say what it is based on |

Page refs use the `=== [PDF page N] ===` markers in `fulltext.txt` (PDF page index, not printed page number). When a quote is used, it is copied verbatim from `fulltext.txt`.

Citation syntax:
- Inside a paper's own `analysis.md`: `(p. N)`.
- Everywhere else (evidence matrix, reports, reviews): pandoc style `[@key, p. N]` or `[@key1; @key2]`. Keys are the folder names under `papers/`. This works with `references.bib` and pandoc.
- `rlab cite-check <project> <file...>` must pass before any written document is handed to the user.

## 2. Never invent
- Every DOI, title, author, year and venue comes from `metadata.json` (resolved by `rlab add` from Crossref/OpenAlex/arXiv/PubMed). Never type a DOI from memory.
- Every finding, number, limitation and quote comes from the paper text. If the paper does not report something, write "not reported".
- Every citation in written output uses an existing paper key in the project. A claim with no source is either removed or labelled [I].
- If something cannot be found or verified, say so plainly. An honest "unknown" beats a plausible guess.

## 3. Source quality tiers
Prefer higher tiers; state the tier when it matters to the argument.

1. Peer-reviewed journal articles and full papers at reputable conferences (`venue_kind: published`); systematic reviews and meta-analyses at the top for evidence synthesis.
2. Peer-reviewed workshop papers, book chapters from academic publishers.
3. Preprints (`venue_kind: preprint`, e.g. arXiv): usable, always flagged "not peer-reviewed". If a published version exists, use it instead.
4. Theses, technical reports, grey literature: background only, flagged.
5. Blogs, news, Wikipedia, vendor material: never cited as evidence. May guide searching.

`venue_kind: published` means the work appeared in a journal or proceedings; it is not proof of rigorous review. Watch for predatory venues (unknown publisher, implausibly fast review, no indexing) and flag them.
Retracted papers (`RETRACTED` flag from `rlab`) are excluded from evidence; mention only as retracted.

## 4. Reading depth
- Detailed methodology, dataset, setup, metrics, findings and limitations require the full text (`evidence_basis: full-text`).
- Abstract-only analysis (`evidence_basis: abstract-only`) may fill objective and headline claims labelled [A] only. All method sections say "full text not available". Abstract-only papers carry less weight in synthesis and gap claims; say so.
- Read the whole paper: methods, results, tables, limitations, appendix if relevant. Note skipped parts in "Analyst notes".

## 5. Critical appraisal checklist
For every empirical paper check and record:
- Sample size and how it was chosen; power or uncertainty reporting.
- Baselines and whether they are fair and current.
- Evaluation design: train/test separation, leakage, cross-validation, held-out data, blinding, control groups.
- Statistical testing: tests, effect sizes, confidence intervals, multiple comparisons.
- Reproducibility: data, code, hyper-parameters, protocol available?
- Conflicts of interest and funding where relevant.
- Whether conclusions go beyond the data (mark those [A] and note it).

Evidence strength: **strong** = adequate N, sound design, replicated or consistent across studies; **moderate** = sound design but single study or limited N; **weak** = small/unclear N, design flaws, abstract-only, or preprint without replication.

## 6. Contradictions
When papers disagree: record both sides in the evidence matrix "Contradictions" section with page refs, then compare data, population, method, metric and time. Offer an explanation only as [I]. Never silently pick a side.

## 7. Research gaps and novelty
A gap is reported only when:
1. It is supported by evidence from analysed papers (explicit future-work statements, consistent limitations, contradictions, untested populations/conditions, missing method comparisons).
2. A dedicated novelty check was run: at least 3 targeted searches (`rlab search`) across at least 2 sources, recent years included, plus a web search for very recent work. Queries, date and closest hits are recorded in the gap entry.
3. Confidence is stated. "No paper found" is phrased as "we found no paper that ... (searches on DATE)", never "this has never been studied".

## 8. Copyright and access
- Download only legal open-access copies: OpenAlex/Unpaywall OA locations, arXiv, Europe PMC, publisher OA pages. `rlab fetch` enforces this and refuses shadow libraries.
- Never bypass paywalls, logins, CAPTCHAs, or rate limits. Never use Sci-Hub, LibGen, Anna's Archive or similar.
- When no OA copy exists: tell the user and ask them to obtain it through their library, then `rlab attach`. Otherwise analyse abstract-only and label it.
- Quotes stay short and attributed. PDFs stay inside the project folder and are not redistributed.

## 9. Preservation
- Original PDFs (`paper.pdf`), extracted text (`fulltext.txt`) and completed analyses (`status: complete`) are never overwritten or deleted without the user's explicit permission. A hook asks the user first (once `setup/claude-settings.json` is installed).
- Analysis status flow: `draft` (in progress) -> `ready` (analyst self-check passed) -> `complete` (critical review passed). Fix review findings while the analysis is `ready`.

# Package Hallucination Attacks on Coding Agents through Prompt Injection in Rule Files

- Authors: Wang, Yupu; Jiang, Zhengyuan; Wang, Reachal; Gong, Neil Zhenqiang
- Year / venue: 2026, arXiv (preprint)
- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2610.09264 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09264
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

Analyst note on scope: this is an attack paper. This analysis records what was measured and how well, for threat-model and defence purposes; it does not reproduce the optimisation procedure in operational detail.

## 1. Research objective
[A] Define a "package hallucination attack" in which an attacker injects a prompt into a community-shared rule file (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules) so that a coding agent replaces a legitimate dependency with an attacker-controlled look-alike package, and propose PackHallu, a black-box optimiser for such injected prompts (p. 1, p. 2). Note: the paper's "package hallucination" is induced substitution of a specific attacker package, not the spontaneous invention of non-existent names studied by most of our corpus (p. 1).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
Not stated as numbered RQs. Implicit questions [I]: (a) are existing prompt-injection attacks effective when embedded in long rule files; (b) does an optimised injected prompt work, and does it transfer across LLMs, agent frameworks and task distributions; (c) do existing prompt-injection detectors catch it (pp. 2–3).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: controlled end-to-end simulation. Agents run in autonomous mode with confirmations disabled; look-alike packages are hosted on a local registry that mirrors PyPI so the agent can `pip install` them on demand (p. 8, p. 10).
- Approach / model / intervention: PackHallu is an evolutionary search that uses a locally run surrogate agent (default: OpenHands + Qwen3-Coder-30B), scores candidates on the agent's full reasoning trajectory rather than only final code, and uses an LLM to critique failed candidates (p. 2, p. 5, p. 8). One prompt is optimised for the numpy pair and reused for other packages by swapping names (p. 12).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: two heuristic attacks (Combined, Repeat) and three optimisation attacks (GCG, ObliInjection — both given white-box access — and TAP) (p. 8, p. 9).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): BigCodeBench (5 third-party packages, 80/20 victim/surrogate split), DS-1000 (pandas, numpy, matplotlib, scipy), RefactorBench (kombu, twisted, urllib3, asgiref, werkzeug) (p. 9, p. 10).
- Sample size (N) and unit: 981, 772 and 43 victim tasks respectively (p. 9); per-package counts e.g. pandas 341, numpy 267 BigCodeBench victim tasks (p. 28). SASR is computed only over tasks where the agent imports the real package under benign conditions (p. 11), and these subset sizes are not reported. [I] Percentages imply much smaller denominators than the task counts (e.g. 98.72% and 1.28% = 77/78 and 1/78 for pandas on Qwen3-Coder-30B, p. 11), so many cells rest on roughly 14–90 tasks.
- Sampling / selection method: tasks grouped by the package they require; RefactorBench packages chosen by frequency (p. 10).
- Data availability (public? link?): no code or data release link found in the paper (searched for repository links and release statements).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: 8 frameworks — OpenHands, OpenCode, Aider, Pi Coding Agent, Cline, Kilo Code, Claude Code, Cursor (p. 8). 13 backbone LLMs, including GPT-5.5, GPT-5.3-Codex, Claude Sonnet 4.6, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Llama-4-Maverick (p. 8, p. 14, p. 16). The look-alike package mirrors the real package's interface and only prints a fixed message when invoked; names use a `_hl` suffix (p. 10). Injection at the start of the rule file by default (p. 12). Search settings R=20, N=3, K=5, T=10 (p. 12).
- Detection: 200 rule files (100 public benign files plus 100 injected counterparts) tested against ProtectAI-DeBERTa, PromptGuard, DataSentinel, PromptArmor (GPT-5 judge) and PIShield (p. 18, p. 19).
- Code availability: not reported.

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- SASR (syntactic attack success rate) — share of tasks where the generated code imports the look-alike package, among tasks that import the real package under benign conditions (p. 11).
- DASR (deployable attack success rate) — additionally requires the code to execute and the look-alike's marker behaviour to run (p. 12). This is closer to real harm than import-only metrics.
- Attention proportion — share of model attention on injected tokens (p. 12, p. 13).
- Detector FNR / FPR (p. 19).
- Statistical testing: Pearson correlations (e.g. r = 0.785 capability vs SASR across LLMs, p. 15; r = −0.186 across frameworks, p. 16); mean ± SD across 5 initialisations (p. 18). No confidence intervals or significance tests for SASR/DASR.

## 7. Key findings
1. Averaged over 5 packages and 5 backbone LLMs on BigCodeBench, PackHallu reached 79.29% SASR and 67.68% DASR; the next-best baseline (Combined Attack) reached 14.99% / 11.35% — [V] (p. 12)
2. More popular packages were harder to substitute (median r = −0.69 between success and PyPI downloads); numpy and scipy were hardest, seaborn easiest — [V] (p. 13)
3. Prompts optimised on one LLM transferred to others in the same framework; 8 of 12 victim LLMs exceeded 90% SASR on at least 3 of 5 packages, e.g. GPT-5.5 97.92% on pandas — [V] (p. 14)
4. More capable backbone LLMs were more susceptible (r = 0.785 between task capability and SASR) — [V] (p. 15)
5. Across frameworks with the same LLM, average SASR was 71.55% and DASR 62.99%, with no relation to capability (r = −0.186) — [V] (p. 15, p. 16)
6. On commercial agents: Cursor 69%–98% SASR; Claude Code with Sonnet 4.6 31.03%–58.95% SASR, the most resistant — [V] (p. 16)
7. Effect weakened as context grew: 53.33% SASR on DS-1000 and 18.60% on repository-level RefactorBench — [V] (p. 16)
8. Claude Code case study (87 numpy tasks): 27 successes (31%); 16 suspicion-based refusals (18.4%); in 33 cases (37.9%) the agent first imported the look-alike, the import failed, and it reverted to numpy instead of running `pip install` — [V] (p. 17, p. 27)
9. No detector was usable: FNR/FPR were ProtectAI 100%/3%, PromptGuard 46%/5%, DataSentinel 49%/16%, PromptArmor 20%/34%, PIShield 21%/11% — [V] (p. 19)

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] No dedicated limitations section. The authors note that a real-world attack would expose users to compromise and contaminate registries, so they used a controlled local registry and benign marker packages (p. 10).
- [A] Repository-level tasks reduce effectiveness because the injected prompt becomes a smaller share of the input (p. 16).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Denominators are not reported; the SASR subset (tasks that import the real package under benign conditions) appears much smaller than the task counts in Table 15.
- [I] Internal inconsistency: the Claude Code case study uses "the whole 87 victim tasks from the numpy subset" (p. 16), while Table 15 lists 267 numpy victim tasks (p. 28).
- [I] Success is reported from a single run per cell; only the initialisation study reports variability (p. 18).
- [I] The look-alike names follow one pattern (`_hl` suffix). The attack substitutes a specific package and does not measure spontaneous hallucination, so its rates must not be compared with the hallucination rates in [@spracklen2024we] or [@spracklen2026llm].
- [I] Autonomous mode with confirmations disabled is a worst case. The paper does not test the default, confirmation-on configuration that many users run.
- [I] The F2 behaviour (agent reverted instead of installing the missing package) shows that DASR depends on whether the agent installs packages on its own. That install decision is not separately measured across agents.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal: surrogate tasks are a disjoint 20% of BigCodeBench (p. 10); in the main experiments the surrogate and victim agent are identical (p. 12), so main-table numbers are a white-box-like upper bound; the transfer tables address this.
- External: Python only; 10 packages; local mirror rather than real PyPI; one injection per rule file.
- Construct: SASR = import of the look-alike; DASR = execution of a benign marker. Neither measures real-world installation from the public registry.
- Statistical conclusion: no CIs; small and unreported per-cell denominators; many comparisons.
- Reproducibility: frameworks and settings are documented in appendix tables (p. 8); code release not reported.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: robust defences for the collaborative rule-file pipeline (p. 20); defences tailored to package hallucination attacks, because general prompt-injection detectors fail (p. 19).
- Suggested by us [I]: (a) an install-time guard that blocks packages that are new, unknown or name-similar to a popular package, which would stop the `_hl`-style substitution regardless of how it was induced; (b) measure how often agents in default mode actually run `pip install` for unknown names (the F2 pattern is evidence they sometimes do not); (c) report denominators and repeated runs.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (exploitability: induced substitution with real agents and a working local registry), RQ3 (prompt-injection detectors as a defence), RQ5 (agent install behaviour; commercial agents tested).
- How it informs our work [I]: this is the closest existing work to G1. It runs real agents (including Claude Code and Cursor) end-to-end against a local PyPI mirror, which is the setup our G1 design proposes. The difference is that here the package is induced by an attacker, whereas G1 asks how often agents spontaneously try to install non-existent packages on ordinary tasks. The F2 finding (agents reverted instead of installing in 37.9% of Claude Code cases) is direct evidence that agent install behaviour varies and must be measured, not assumed. For G2, the detector table shows that checking the instruction file is not enough, which supports a guard at the install step.

## 14. Key quotes
> "a package hallucination attack causes the agent to import a specific package chosen and controlled by the attacker." (p. 1)
> "Rather than attempting to pip install the missing package, the victim agent reverts to numpy and proceeds" (p. 17)
> "no existing detector reliably identifies our attack while maintaining a usable FPR." (p. 19)

- Uncertainties: per-cell denominators; the 87 vs 267 numpy-task inconsistency.

# Harmless Yet Harmful: Neutral Prompting Attacks for Stealthy Hallucination Steering in Agent Skills

- Authors: Hsu, Chia-Yi; Yu, Chia-Mu; Huang, Chun-Ying; Sakuma, Jun
- Year / venue: 2026, Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026 (published)
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

Analyst note on scope: this is an attack paper. This analysis records what was measured and how well, for threat-model and defence purposes; it does not reproduce the optimisation prompts or example Skills in the appendix.

## 1. Research objective
[A] Show that semantically benign Skill instructions (encouraging imagination, completeness, exhaustive exploration) can raise package hallucination and fake-package install commands in coding agents without any explicit malicious intent or target package. The paper calls this a Neutral Prompting Attack (NPA) (p. 1, p. 2). It positions itself against targeted Dependency Steering [@liu2026trust], which leaves package-specific evidence (p. 1).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
Stated by the authors (p. 2):
- RQ1: Can benign prompts amplify package hallucination and installation risk?
- RQ2: Does NPA generalise across models?
- RQ3: How does NPA affect the distribution and exploitability of hallucinated packages?
- RQ4: Can NPA evade existing defences?
- RQ5: Which prompt properties contribute most?

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: controlled experiment on the Spracklen benchmark plus closed-loop agent runs (pp. 4–5).
- Approach / model / intervention: evolutionary search over Skill variants with three LLM-driven edit operators (rewrite a section, inject a section, change framing), scored by the share of hallucinated packages in a shadow model's outputs; NPA-Stealth adds penalties for suspicion and utility loss (pp. 3–4).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: Normal Skill (a public Python-patterns Skill from the SkillsMP marketplace) and IP (Illusionist's Prompt, a prior hallucination-inducing prompt method) (p. 5).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): the four prompt sets of [@spracklen2024we] (p. 4, p. 5).
- Sample size (N) and unit: 5% of prompts for optimisation, 95% for evaluation per dataset (p. 5); absolute prompt counts are not restated. Agent runs use "separate task configurations" whose sizes are not reported (p. 5). Human study: 10 computer-science students (p. 8).
- Sampling / selection method: benchmark reuse; human raters recruited from university labs (p. 8).
- Data availability (public? link?): not reported. The authors deliberately avoid revealing complete fake package names (p. 10).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: decoding and evaluation follow the Spracklen benchmark (p. 5); 50 generations, 20 mutations per generation, beam size 15; about 16–18 minutes per generation on NVIDIA H100/H200 GPUs (p. 5). Package names checked against PyPI; standard-library modules excluded (p. 4, p. 5). One optimisation run per setting (p. 5).
- Agents: Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenHands. Generated hallucination, proposed install and executed install were measured in separate task configurations, not as one pipeline (p. 5).
- Runtime safeguards tested: package existence check, registry lookup, allowlist, environment resolution (p. 8). The implementation of these safeguards is not described in the main text or appendix (Appendix E covers only the Skill scanners, p. 50).
- Code availability: not reported.

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Hallucination ASR — share of evaluated responses containing at least one package not found on PyPI (p. 5).
- Pip Install ASR — share of responses whose `pip install` commands contain at least one non-existent package (p. 5).
- Agent metrics — generated hallucination, proposed install and executed install rates (p. 6).
- Exploitability audit — unique names, registerable share, persistence across 4 models and 3 prompts, share appearing in install commands, plausibility (p. 7).
- Statistical testing: none reported; single optimisation run per setting (p. 5).

## 7. Key findings
1. With the benign Skill, Hallucination ASR on Qwen2.5-Coder-32B was 3.53% (LLM_AT) and 4.54% (LLM_LY); NPA raised these to 57.76% and 78.99% — [V] (p. 5, p. 6)
2. Effects varied a lot by model: Qwen2.5-Coder-14B rose only from 5.21% to 12.32% on LLM_AT; Nemotron-3-Nano had a high baseline (35.58%–50.20%) — [V] (p. 6)
3. In real agents, with the benign Skill, executed installs of non-existent packages were 3.33% (Claude Code), 1.05% (OpenCode) and 1.11% (OpenHands); with NPA they were 90.77%, 60.34% and 82.29%; with NPA-Stealth 27.99%–42.52% — [V] (p. 5, p. 6)
4. NPA Skills optimised on Qwen2.5-Coder-32B transferred to GPT-5 (Hallucination ASR 1.28% to 29.29%) but barely to Llama-3.1-8B (16.43% to 17.74%) — [V] (p. 6)
5. NPA concentrated hallucinations onto repeated names: unique-name share fell from 73.7% (Normal) to 54.4%; cross-model persistence across 4 models was 24.17% vs 0%–4.47% for other conditions; over 96% of names were registerable — [V] (p. 6, p. 7)
6. Static Skill scanners did not flag NPA Skills; only Snyk Agent Scan did, and an NPA variant optimised against Snyk evaded it while still raising hallucination — [V] (p. 7)
7. Package-existence check, registry lookup and environment resolution left Hallucination/Pip ASR near the unprotected level (about 50%–60%); only a strict allowlist reduced both to 0% — [V] (p. 8)
8. In the blind human rating (n=10), NPA scored 5.0/7 suspicion and only 50% would enable it, while NPA-Stealth scored 1.2/7 and 100% would enable it, the same as the benign Skill — [V] (p. 8)
9. "Creativity" wording drove most of the effect (44.60% alone); "exhaustiveness" alone had no effect (3.57%) — [V] (p. 8)

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Python only; JavaScript, Rust and other ecosystems not evaluated (p. 10).
- [A] Output-level evaluation only; no mechanistic analysis (p. 10).
- [A] Not every hallucinated name is immediately exploitable; real risk depends on registration availability, user trust and installation behaviour (p. 10).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] The runtime-safeguard result (finding 7) is hard to interpret. An existence check should, by definition, stop installation of names not on PyPI, yet Pip Install ASR stayed at 51.12%. The metric seems to count fake names in generated commands, not installs that succeed after the check, and the safeguard implementation is not described. This finding should not be read as "existence checks do not work".
- [I] One optimisation run per setting and no variance or confidence intervals; agent task-set sizes are not reported.
- [I] Results are sensitive to model choice (finding 2) and to the base Skill; only one marketplace Skill was used as the starting point.
- [I] The human study is small (10 students) and not representative of developers who install Skills.
- [I] Compute (H100/H200, about 15 hours per optimisation) means the attack is expensive to construct, but the resulting Skill is cheap to use.
- [I] Positive: unlike most of our corpus, this paper reports executed installs in real agents under a benign Skill, which gives a baseline rate for unattacked agents.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal: shadow model equals victim model in the main results (p. 5), so main numbers are an upper bound; transfer is tested separately (pp. 6–7).
- External: Python/PyPI only; one base Skill; three agents; open models plus GPT-5 for transfer only.
- Construct: Hallucination ASR uses PyPI existence at evaluation time; the date of the PyPI check is not reported, so names registered later (including by squatters) may be misclassified.
- Statistical conclusion: no tests; single runs; small human sample.
- Reproducibility: hyper-parameters are reported (p. 5) and prompt templates are in the appendix; no code or data release is stated.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: extend to other ecosystems; mechanistic analysis (p. 10); defences beyond content scanning, such as runtime package verification, registry-aware generation, dependency allowlists, grounded retrieval over package indices, and behavioural auditing of Skills (p. 9, p. 10).
- Suggested by us [I]: (a) test a correctly implemented install-time guard (block non-existent, very new or maintainer-less packages before `pip install` runs) and report blocked installs rather than generated names; (b) measure baseline executed-install rates on larger task sets without any malicious Skill (finding 3 is a first data point); (c) audit agent instruction files for creativity-style wording as a cheap heuristic.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (baseline hallucination for 4 models), RQ2 (repeatable, registerable names; cross-model persistence), RQ3 (scanners and runtime safeguards), RQ5 (agent install behaviour measured in Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenHands).
- How it informs our work [I]: this paper narrows G1. It already reports executed installs of non-existent packages by three real agents under a benign Skill (1.05%–3.33%). G1 must therefore be positioned as a larger, more realistic measurement (more tasks, default agent settings, a logging registry proxy, natural rather than benchmark prompts), not as the first measurement. It also matters for G2: its runtime-safeguard table is the only prior evaluation of existence checks in this setting, and its method is unclear. A transparent, reproducible benchmark of install-time guards (G2) would directly resolve that. Finally, because benign-sounding instructions can raise hallucination, model-side defences alone are insufficient, which strengthens the case for the install-time layer.

# Trust Me, Import This: Dependency Steering Attacks via Malicious Agent Skills

- Authors: Liu, Yiyong; Hsu, Chia-Yi; Huang, Chun-Ying; Backes, Michael; Wen, Rui; Yu, Chia-Mu
- Year / venue: 2026, arXiv (preprint)
- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2605.09594 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09594
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

Analyst note on scope: this is an attack paper. This analysis records what was measured and how well, for threat-model and defence purposes; it does not reproduce the optimisation procedure in operational detail.

## 1. Research objective
[A] Show that package hallucination is not only a passive model error but can be actively induced: a malicious persistent instruction artifact ("Skill", e.g. SKILL.md, Cursor Rules) can bias a coding agent toward an attacker-chosen package during benign coding tasks, without changing model weights, training data or the user's prompt (p. 1). The paper calls this "Dependency Steering" (p. 1, p. 3).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
Not stated as numbered RQs. Implicit questions [I]: (a) does a Skill that names a target package raise how often that package appears in generated dependencies; (b) does optimising the Skill text raise it further while keeping the Skill plausible; (c) does the effect transfer across models, prompts and domains; (d) do existing Skill scanners detect such Skills (pp. 2–3, 9–12).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: controlled black-box experiment on open-weight models; three attack conditions compared against a benign-Skill baseline (pp. 4–7).
- Approach / model / intervention: (1) direct injection — the Skill explicitly recommends the target package (p. 4); (2) Bayesian optimisation over a fixed set of semantic mutation operators, refined by a genetic algorithm (p. 4); (3) the authors' method, adapted from the AutoDAN-Turbo jailbreak framework: an LLM-generated patch appended to an otherwise benign Skill, scored by an LLM judge on target inclusion, stealth and fluency, with a strategy library reused across rounds (p. 5).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: benign Skill (general hallucination rate, Table I, p. 7); direct injection (Table II, p. 7); Bayesian optimisation (Table III, p. 8).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): the four prompt sets from Spracklen et al. — LLM-generated and Stack Overflow prompts, each in all-time and last-year variants (p. 6). This links the paper directly to [@spracklen2024we].
- Sample size (N) and unit: prompts filtered to those about the source package (default `requests`), split 90% optimisation / 10% evaluation (p. 6). The absolute number of test prompts is not reported. [I] The reported percentages are consistent with small, model-dependent denominators (e.g. 78.57% = 11/14, 93.55% = 29/31, 97.30% = 36/37; Table IV, p. 8), so each cell probably rests on roughly 14–40 outputs.
- Sampling / selection method: filtering by source package; no further detail (p. 6).
- Data availability (public? link?): not reported. No code or artifact link found in the paper.

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: five open-weight models — Llama-3.1-8B, Phi-4-mini, Qwen2.5-Coder 7B/14B/32B (p. 6). Target temperature 0.6, top_p 0.9; proxy LLM temperature 0.7; one completion per test prompt (p. 6). Bayesian optimisation used a 300-iteration budget; the authors' method used 10 iterations per target (p. 6). Main results use the "Unconstrained Mode" (stealth and fluency weights set to 0, veto off), i.e. they maximise inclusion only (p. 6). Only Python tasks (p. 6). The default target name is a non-existent, benign placeholder package (p. 6).
- Detection test: 3 static scanners, 4 LLM/agent-based auditors and 1 commercial sandbox (SandyClaw) (p. 11); an adaptive variant feeds scanner feedback back into optimisation on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B (p. 12).
- Code availability: not reported.

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Targeted hallucination rate (THR) — share of benign prompts whose dependency-related output (imports, `pip install`, requirements entries) contains the attacker-chosen package (p. 3, p. 6). It measures attack success at the generation step only.
- General hallucination rate (GHR) — share of outputs containing any non-existent package other than the target (p. 6).
- Detection outcome per scanner: detected / not detected / "low" severity (Table IX, p. 12).
- Statistical testing: none. Repeated-run variability is reported only as a standard deviation not exceeding 6.5% (p. 11). No confidence intervals or significance tests.

## 7. Key findings
1. With a benign Skill, general hallucination rates were 0%–32.37%; Phi-4-mini on LLM_LY was highest; Qwen2.5-Coder 14B/32B were at or near 0% on several sets — [V] (p. 7)
2. Direct injection (Skill openly recommends the package) reached THR of 1.52%–87.50%; Qwen2.5-Coder models were most susceptible (e.g. 32B: 87.50% on LLM_AT) — [V] (p. 7)
3. The optimised attack reached THR of 21.43%–100%; Qwen2.5-Coder-32B: 100% (LLM_AT), 97.30%, 62.07%, 63.50%; Llama-3.1-8B: 78.57% on LLM_AT — [V] (p. 8)
4. Lookalike names close to a real package (e.g. a one-letter typo of `requests`) were often auto-corrected by the model under the baselines (0% on Qwen2.5-Coder-14B) but reached 61%–100% under the optimised attack — [V] (p. 8, p. 9)
5. Optimised Skills transferred across models (many Qwen cells above 80%) and across domains, and test-prompt THR was comparable to training-prompt THR — [A] (p. 9, p. 10)
6. Hiding the package name completely (explicitness levels 4–5) dropped THR to 0%; the name must appear in some form for the attack to work — [V] (p. 10)
7. Longer Skills diluted the effect for most models (e.g. Qwen2.5-Coder-7B 89.66% short vs 27.59% long) — [V] (p. 11)
8. All three static scanners missed the Skills (one rated them "low"); among LLM/agent auditors only Snyk Agent Red Teaming detected them; the sandbox (SandyClaw) detected all five — [V] (p. 12)
9. With scanner feedback in the loop, the Skill evaded Snyk and was downgraded by SandyClaw, at a THR of 65.52% on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B — [A] (p. 12)

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Only open-source models; closed commercial agents were not tested (p. 12).
- [A] The prompt distribution cannot fully represent real software-engineering workflows (p. 12).
- [A] Measures dependency generation, not end-to-end compromise after installation (p. 12).
- [A] Future defences designed for persistent steering may be stronger (p. 12).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Small and unreported test sets: N=1 completion on a 10% split, with percentages implying roughly 14–40 outputs per cell; differences of 5–10 points are within noise.
- [I] Main results use Unconstrained Mode (stealth weight 0). The stealth claims and the detection test may therefore apply to different Skills than the headline THRs; the paper does not state which mode produced the Skills in Table IX.
- [I] The models are 8B–32B open-weight models served directly, not agents with tool use. "Coding agent" in the title is broader than what was tested.
- [I] The judge, attacker and scorer are LLMs; the scoring rubric and proxy models are not fully specified, which limits reproducibility.
- [I] Reference [36] for "Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct" is a security-tuned Llama derivative's technical report (p. 15), so the exact model checkpoint is ambiguous.
- [I] Minor reporting errors: the THR definition is cited as Section IV-C but appears in Section III-A (p. 3, p. 6); one Table I value lacks a % sign (p. 7).
- [I] Detection is reported as binary per model, without false-positive rates of the scanners on benign Skills.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal: the same benchmark family is used to optimise and evaluate (90/10 split); the risk of leakage across near-duplicate prompts is not discussed.
- External: Python only; five open-weight models; one placeholder target name by default; no real IDE agent or closed model.
- Construct: THR counts any appearance of the name in dependency outputs (mention, import or install command), not an actual install. That is appropriate for a generation-step attack but overstates installation risk.
- Statistical conclusion: no CIs or tests; small denominators; single completion per prompt (only the stability check repeats runs, p. 11).
- Reproducibility: no code or data link found; hyper-parameters are partly reported (p. 6).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: defences designed specifically against persistent behavioural steering (p. 12); the attack is argued to generalise to other persistent instruction artifacts such as Cursor/Windsurf rules and repository instruction files (p. 12).
- Suggested by us [I]: (a) measure whether a pre-install guard (registry existence + metadata checks, as in [@raj2026names]) blocks the steered package at install time, which is independent of how the name was induced; (b) test closed agents with real tool use; (c) report scanner false-positive rates on benign Skills.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (baseline hallucination rates for 5 open models), RQ2 (exploitability: an attacker can induce a chosen name rather than wait for one), RQ3 (Skill scanners as a defence and how they fail), RQ5 (agent instruction files as an untested attack surface for client-side guards).
- How it informs our work [I]: this changes the threat model behind G2. If an attacker can make an agent emit a specific package name on demand, defences that only rely on the model not hallucinating are insufficient; an install-time check (does the package exist, is it new, does it have maintainers and a repository) is the layer that still applies. It also shows that static Skill scanners missed these Skills, which supports evaluating guards at the package-install step rather than at the instruction-file step.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | With a benign Skill, general hallucination rates for 5 open models were 0%–32.37% (highest Phi-4-mini on LLM_LY; Qwen2.5-Coder 14B/32B near 0%) | 7 | V | weak |
| RQ2 | A Skill that openly recommends a non-existent package makes models emit it in 1.52%–87.50% of benign prompts | 7 | V | weak |
| RQ2 | An optimised malicious Skill raised targeted hallucination to 21%–100% (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B: 100% on LLM_AT) | 8 | V | weak |
| RQ2 | Typo-like target names were auto-corrected under the baselines but not under the optimised attack | 8, 9 | V | weak |

| RQ5 | Only open-weight models without tool use were tested; closed commercial agents and end-to-end installation were not | 12 | A | moderate |

## 14. Key quotes
> "we show that this risk is not only a passive model failure. It can be actively induced through the persistent Skill artifact." (p. 1)
> "our evaluation mainly measures dependency-generation behavior rather than full end-to-end compromise after malicious package installation." (p. 12)
> "To avoid causing real-world harm, we do not publish or deploy any malicious packages." (p. 14)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: whole paper read (pp. 1–16), including appendix A–C. References skimmed.
- Uncertainties: absolute test-set sizes; which optimisation mode produced the Skills used in the detection test; exact Llama checkpoint.
- Ethics: the authors used benign placeholder packages and did not publish malicious packages (p. 14).
